newsitem.title: BRAZIL: INSTANT VIEW - Brazil Sept trade gap $655 million.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Brazil Sept trade gap $655 million.

text.p: Following are comments from economists in Brazil in reaction to September's larger-than- expected $655 million trade deficit. The government announced imports totalling $4.77 billion and exports at $4.115 billion for the month. The market had expected a deficit of about $400 million.

MATTHEW MONIOT, economist at Rio de Janeiro investment bank FONTE CINDAM: "The number is well above market expectations. This is a moderately negative number demonstrating a clear trend toward deteriorating trade accounts."
Moniot added that the larger-than-expected import figure was likely the result of growing demand for consumer and capital goods, triggered by a steady uptick in the economy.
ARMANDO GONCALVES, economist at Sao Paulo-based UNIBANCO: "It was considerably above what we had expected, but we've got to see the breakdown."

He said one factor for the large gap could be a sharp increase in oil import tax receipts in September which had doubled over August. "That could be a sign that (state oil monopoly) Petrobras could be stocking up fearing a strike ahead of wage negotiations in October," Goncalves said.

Goncalves said the higher than expected trade gap might also be explained by the fact that companies had brought forward their raw material purchases, in order to organize production previous to the holiday sales at the end of the year.
"1996 is unlike the previous two years in that companies have had time to organize themselves better and schedule their purchases before the year-end rush," he said.
Goncalves said the latest trade figures should not be any cause for alarm. He said Unibanco expected the trade account to end the year with a deficit of around $3 billion.
DANY RAPPAPORT, chief economist, MCM Consultores in Brazil: "This number is big, but it's not the big surprise. October will be even worse."

Rappaport noted that despite September's larger-than- expected gap, the month did not see a tremendous amount of imports by retailers preparing for the Christmas season. He said the bulk of Christmas imports would come in October and November.
"We're raising our year-end trade deficit forecast to about $4 billion from $3.5 billion," Rappaport said.
